item.text: {"text":"GRU4Rec’s established BPR-max loss addresses weak gradients from averaging many easy negatives: softmax weights over negative scores emphasize difficult candidates, with negative-score regularization. The official implementation also supports popularity-tempered sampling and logQ-corrected cross-entropy, making these direct comparisons within the existing GRU backbone. [Original paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), [official implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec). A 2024 sequential-recommendation study compared random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling; results varied by dataset and item popularity, providing no universal argument for harder negatives. [Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276).\n\nFalse-negative handling and sampling correction solve different problems. UFNRec (SDM 2023) identifies potential false negatives, reverses their labels and controls noise through output-space EMA and consistency regularization; high model scores alone do not establish true relevance. [UFNRec](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611977653.ch6). A RecSys 2025 paper refines logQ correction because the positive is always included, whereas negatives are sampled; correction must reflect the actual sampling scheme. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331). Practical hypothesis: hold positional weighting and architecture fixed, compare regularized BPR-max against sampled cross-entropy, then separately vary negative count and uniform/popularity mixture. Use training histories to exclude known positives; treat tempered hard-negative weighting as an experimental safeguard, not verified false-negative detection. Deterministic top-k mining cannot simply inherit the original proposal probabilities for importance correction. Keep one trained GRU model per category and select through the pinned macro validation HR@10; stronger training margins alone establish no validation gain."}
